title: Short Stuff: Longyou Caves
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Longyou Caves (spelled "long U" in the transcript), a system of 24 carved underground grottos in Quzhou/Jiujiang area of China (the hosts say "Jujiang province"), rediscovered in 1992 after villagers drained flooded ponds with water pumps over seventeen days. The hosts cover the discovery, the staircases and carved pillars and wall texture, estimated age of about two thousand years based on pottery in silt, the lack of historical records, the single-entrance chambers and drainage channels, the labor estimate for excavation, skepticism about relief carvings possibly being modern, and theories (mine, palace, garrison, cistern) that they find lacking.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh welcomes listeners to Short Stuff and introduces the topic of the Long U caves with Chuck.

segments.title: Discovery of the flooded ponds
segments.summary: Villagers near ponds in a Chinese province in 1992 were told of bottomless ponds; a man named Wu had the village pump out one pond over seventeen days. Five deep ponds were drained, revealing carved staircases descending into darkness. The hosts note the ponds had no fish and the giant-fish story is doubtful.

segments.title: Number and scale of the caves
segments.summary: Twenty-four grottos were found in total, five major and nineteen smaller, covering seven and a half acres. The largest has a ceiling about one hundred feet high, held up by carved pillars.

segments.title: Carved walls and chisel marks
segments.summary: The walls, ceilings and pillars are covered in parallel carved lines creating a uniform textured background, with smaller chisel marks angled at about sixty degrees. The hosts conclude human hands shaped the caves.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break before returning to the age of the caves.

segments.title: Age and lack of records
segments.summary: The caves are estimated at about two thousand years old, based on pottery found in silt on the floor when drained, dated to around the reign of Emperor Swan of the Han dynasty. No Chinese records document their construction or purpose; the only mention is a seventeenth-century poem by Yushun.

segments.title: Hua Shan Grottos comparison and single-entrance chambers
segments.summary: The Long U caves do not match other Chinese quarries, grottos, or palaces. The Hua Shan Grottos are a similar mystery built about fifteen hundred years later. Each cave has only one entrance, with shared walls only a couple of feet thick, and drainage channels to a central pool that flooded as the drains stopped working.

segments.title: Carving precision and labor estimate
segments.summary: The hosts marvel at how the builders carved adjacent chambers without breaking through shared walls. They believe the caves were carved downward layer by layer with small tools. An estimate from Interesting Engineering says removing the rock would take about 1,000 people six years working around the clock.

segments.title: Missing rock and relief carvings
segments.summary: The million cubic meters of removed siltstone has never been located, and no tools were found. Bas relief art in the caves is thought to have been carved much later.

segments.title: Skepticism about relief carvings and cistern theory
segments.summary: Skeptical sources suggest the bas reliefs were carved after the 1990s drainage to attract tourists, a possible misunderstanding of the site. The hosts review theories: a mine, a palace, and a troop garrison, all found unconvincing. A video theory that they were cisterns is considered plausible by some commenters.

segments.title: Why the cistern theory fails
segments.summary: The hosts say the cistern idea does not hold water, mainly because the intricate carvings would be pointless in a water storage cistern. They conclude the caves remain largely a mystery.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing remarks and iHeartRadio production credit.
